message.content:
Re-skin the self-hosted "Nxeon Mail" webmail (SOGo, inside Mailcow) to match the Nxeon brand — dark navy + violet, like the customer portal. The mail server is a separate VM at **10.20.0.10** running mailcow-dockerized. This host can reach it; SSH in with `ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new root@10.20.0.10` (an SSH key/access was used for the earlier partial rebrand — if password is needed, check /etc/nxeon/ or /root for a mailcow/VM credential file first). Everything you do happens ON THAT VM, not in /opt/nxeon. Do NOT touch /opt/nxeon, do NOT run git.

Context: the login page is already lightly branded ("Nxeon Mail" logo, dark). The problem is the rest of the SOGo webmail interface (inbox, buttons, toolbars) is stock — a bright green Login button, generic grey UI. The owner wants the whole webmail to look like Nxeon: dark navy background (~#0a0e1a / #0f1526), violet/brand accent (~#8a70fb / gradient to #a78bfa), white/slate text, replace the green primary buttons with the violet brand.

Do this on the VM:
1. Locate the mailcow install (usually `/opt/mailcow-dockerized`). Find how SOGo custom theming is injected — mailcow supports SOGo UI customization via `data/conf/sogo/` (e.g. `custom-theme.css`, `sogo.conf` `SOGoUIxDebugEnabled`/theme, or a `data/web/css/` include) and the login/branding under `data/conf/nginx/` or `data/web/`. Read the existing partial-rebrand files to see what's already themed and extend from there.
2. **Back up** any file before editing (`cp x x.bak-$(date)`). Write a custom CSS theme that restyles the SOGo webmail app (not just login): backgrounds, the top toolbar, the folder tree, the message list, buttons (turn the green primary into the violet brand gradient), links, and the compose view — a cohesive dark-navy/violet look. Inject it so SOGo actually serves it (via the mailcow SOGo custom CSS mechanism; if needed, mount it into the sogo-mailcow container and reference it, or append to the served theme file).
3. Apply + reload: restart the relevant container(s) (`docker compose restart sogo-mailcow nginx-mailcow` or `mailcow` equivalent from the install dir) and clear the SOGo/memcached theme cache if applicable.
4. **Verify safely**: after restart, confirm the webmail still loads (`curl -sk https://127.0.0.1/SOGo/ -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` on the VM, or via mail.nxeon.cloud) and returns a normal response (not 500). If anything breaks, restore from your .bak and report. Do NOT leave the mail server broken.

Report: exactly which files you changed on the VM, how the CSS is injected/served, the container(s) restarted, and the post-change webmail HTTP status. If SOGo's theming can't be fully applied via CSS and needs a deeper approach (e.g. a theme package), say so clearly rather than half-doing it.

Done. The Nxeon dark-navy/violet reskin is live on the SOGo webmail and both containers are healthy with no errors.

## What I found
The earlier partial rebrand relied on `data/conf/sogo/custom-theme.js` (an Angular Material `$mdThemingProvider` theme mounted to `WebServerResources/js/theme.js`). **That file is dead** — nothing in SOGo's templates or JS bundles ever references `theme.js`, so it was never loaded. That's why the app stayed stock (teal toolbars, green Login/primary buttons). SOGo's real theming comes from two CSS files loaded in `UIxPageFrame.wox` / `SOGoRootPage.wox`: `css/theme-default.css` (Angular Material colors — the green `rgb(86,176,76)` accent and teal `rgb(77,128,128)` primary) then `css/styles.css` (structure). nginx serves these from the shared `sogo-web-vol-1` volume, which SOGo's `bootstrap-sogo.sh` repopulates on every start via `rsync -a /usr/local/lib/GNUstep/SOGo/. /sogo_web/`.

## What I changed (all on VM 10.20.0.10, under `/opt/mailcow-dockerized`)
- **`data/conf/sogo/nxeon-sogo-override.css`** (new) — the ~7.7 KB Nxeon override block: dark-navy backgrounds (`#0a0e1a`/`#0f1526`/panels `#111a2e`), violet gradient (`#8a70fb → #a78bfa`) replacing the green/teal on the toolbar, primary + accent + FAB buttons, light slate text (`#e6ebf5`), restyled folder tree/sidenav, message list rows, menus/dialogs/autocomplete, inputs and the compose/CKEditor body, links, dividers, progress, badges and scrollbars.
- **`data/conf/sogo/custom-styles.css`** (new) — pristine `styles.css` (extracted from the container) **+** the override appended, so it loads *after* `theme-default.css` and wins the cascade (also uses `!important` to beat the few hardcoded `#fff` backgrounds).
- **`data/conf/sogo/custom-styles.css.orig`** (new) — untouched backup of the original `styles.css` (875,726 bytes).
- **`docker-compose.override.yml`** (new) — bind-mounts `custom-styles.css` over `…/WebServerResources/css/styles.css` in the `sogo-mailcow` service. Verified via `docker compose config` that this *adds* to (does not replace) the base volume list — all original mounts (`/etc/sogo`, `/sogo_web`, logos, `theme.js`, etc.) remain intact.

## How it's injected/served
File-swap, mirroring the existing proven pattern (they already bind-mount `theme.js` and the logos the same way): the mounted `styles.css` gets rsynced into the shared `sogo-web-vol-1` on SOGo start, and nginx serves it. No request-handling/proxy changes, so it can't break mail flow, and it's fully reversible (delete the override mount + restart).

## Applied & verified
- Restarted: **`sogo-mailcow`** (recreated — required to pick up the new mount) and **`nginx-mailcow`**.
- Login page `https://127.0.0.1/SOGo/` → **HTTP 200**; app `/SOGo/so/` → **HTTP 200** (no 500).
- Served `styles.css` is now **883,447 bytes**, contains the `NXEON MAIL` block and `#8a70fb`, and the shared-volume copy confirms the bootstrap rsync propagated it.
- Both containers `Up`, no errors in SOGo logs.

## One caveat worth noting
Because this swaps the whole `styles.css`, a future mailcow/SOGo update that changes the upstream `styles.css` won't reach the app (my copy shadows it). To re-sync after an update: re-extract the container's new `styles.css` to `custom-styles.css.orig`, re-append `nxeon-sogo-override.css`, and restart `sogo-mailcow`. This was a deliberate trade for the lowest-risk, non-breaking method; the pixel-perfect alternative (regenerating Angular Material's compiled `theme-default.css`) is far more fragile and wasn't necessary — the CSS override fully achieves the dark-navy/violet look including turning the green primary/Login button into the violet brand gradient.
